hero.title: Map the Customer Experience.
hero.intro: Turn Lesson 42’s essential feature set into a clear customer path, with decisions, recovery, accessibility and observable completion.

sections.label: 01 / WATCH
sections.heading: How does a customer complete the core task?

scenes.title: Start with one task
scenes.visual: Task card connected to Lesson 42 matrix
scenes.narration: A user flow shows how a customer moves through a task. Start with the customer, context and essential features selected in Lesson 42. Mapping a flow does not prove demand or usability.

scenes.title: Define the entry
scenes.narration: Write what brings the customer here and what must already be true. In our fictional registration-route mock-up, the customer opens a sample invitation. No real registration or payment is connected.

scenes.title: Map actions and responses
scenes.narration: For each step, write what the customer does and what the system shows. Connect each step to an essential feature ID. Keep the main path small and leave deferred features outside this flow.

scenes.title: Add decisions and recovery
scenes.visual: Decision diamond, error and exit branches
scenes.narration: A complete flow includes decisions, empty states and errors. If an option is unavailable, explain the next safe action. Include cancel and recovery paths so the customer does not reach a dead end.

scenes.title: Check access and completion
scenes.narration: Check keyboard access, readable labels, language direction and necessary data at each relevant step. Define what successful task completion looks like. These are planned checks, not a claim that testing has passed.

scenes.title: Prepare the handoff
scenes.narration: Export your user flow with step IDs, feature links, branches and unresolved dependencies. Lesson 44 uses it to choose a product-building approach. Later prototype and usability work will test these assumptions.

sections.label: 02 / LEARN
sections.heading: Show the path from entry to completion.

children: A
user flow
maps one task through customer actions, system responses and branches. An
entry point
starts the task. A
decision
changes the path. A
recovery state
helps someone continue or exit safely.
Objective:
create a scoped flow connected to your essential features.
Why it matters:
features alone do not explain how someone completes a task or what happens when something goes wrong.
Review your Lesson 41 MVP scope and Lesson 42 essential features.
Identify the customer, trigger, entry point and starting conditions.
Number each customer action and system response; link feature IDs.
Add decisions, alternate paths, empty/error states, cancel and recovery.
Check accessibility, language and necessary data at relevant steps.
Define completion and unresolved dependencies for Lesson 44.
Fictional example: registration-route mock-up

Invitation → sample event details (F01) → choose available route (F02) → review destination (F03). If no route is available, show an explanation and return/exit choice. Cancel returns to details without pretending to save a registration. Success means the correct sample destination is shown. Loyalty points and payment remain excluded. This flow is planned and untested.

A flow describes behaviour; a screen wireframe describes layout. This lesson creates the flow. Lesson 45 creates a prototype, and Lesson 46 tests usability. Keep customer evidence, technical feasibility and privacy obligations explicitly unresolved where they are unknown.
Review Lesson 42 feature priorities

children: Map one core task. Use numbered rows and arrows in text: S01 | open invitation | show details | F01 → S02. Record each branch with its condition and destination. You can draw a diagram separately; this prototype saves structured text.
Local autosave only; plaintext browser storage. Use anonymous planning notes.
